books.section: Great Depression and the New Deal (1929-1939)

primary_sources: Herbert Hoover, address accepting the Republican presidential nomination, August 11, 1928

stimulus.text: “We in America today are nearer to the final triumph over poverty than ever before in the history of any land. The poorhouse is vanishing from among us. We have not yet reached the goal, but, given a chance to go forward with the policies of the last 8 years, we shall soon with the help of God be in sight of the day when poverty will be banished from this Nation.” — Herbert Hoover, speech accepting the Republican presidential nomination, August 11, 1928. Abridged.
stimulus.source_note: Herbert Hoover, address accepting the Republican presidential nomination, Stanford, California, August 11, 1928. Verbatim excerpt, abridged; public domain.

source: original; stimulus verbatim from Herbert Hoover, address accepting the Republican presidential nomination, August 11, 1928, public domain
stem: Within four years of Hoover's statement, which of the following had happened?

options.text: The New Deal had ended the Great Depression
options.misconception: The New Deal began in 1933, after Hoover left office, and it did not end the Depression. Wartime spending did that.

options.text: The Federal Reserve had been abolished by Congress
options.misconception: The Federal Reserve was never abolished. It still exists today.
Unemployment moved the other way. It reached about 25 percent by 1933.

options.text: About one worker in four was unemployed

rationales.A: Background from the books: the New Deal began under Roosevelt in 1933 and never ended the Depression; entry into World War II did.
rationales.B: Background from the books: the Federal Reserve, created in 1913, survived the Depression and still operates today.
rationales.C: Background from the books: unemployment rose from 3.2 percent in 1929 to 24.9 percent in 1933, not below 5 percent.
rationales.D: Background from the books: by 1933 the unemployment rate stood at 24.9 percent, about one worker in four.
rationales.general:
1. Fix the date: four years after 1928 is 1932, the depth of the Depression.
2. Ask what life looked like then. Background from the books: banks were failing and about one worker in four had no job.
3. Check the other options: the New Deal had not begun, the Federal Reserve still stood, and unemployment had risen, not fallen.
4. Within four years, about one worker in four was unemployed.
Remember: a promise from a boom year is tested by the bust, so count the years and check the facts.
